messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  (none)

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  (none)

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

John, a 57-year-old interior designer from North America, has been struggling with intense anxiety and distress since he survived a life-threatening car accident several months ago. The trauma of that day continues to linger in his daily life, manifesting through vivid triggers and pervasive negative appraisals. On the fateful day of the accident, John was driving home from a client meeting when another vehicle ran a red light, colliding with his car head-on. The impact shattered the windshield, and the sound of metal twisting and groaning still echoes in his mind whenever he hears any car sounds. He recalls the overwhelming sensation of fear as his body reacted involuntarily, trying to brace for the inevitable crash. Since then, even the slightest noise of a car engine or screeching tires sends him into a state of heightened alertness. John’s triggers extend beyond auditory cues; the mere discussion of accidents can elicit intense anxiety and flashbacks. He recently had a meeting with a client who mentioned an incident involving their vehicle, and John found himself struggling to maintain his composure. The conversation sent waves of distress through him, triggering memories of that fateful day. The accident has left John feeling profoundly uncertain about his own body's reliability. "I can no longer trust my own body," he had come to believe, haunted by the sense of vulnerability and unpredictability it brought on. This lack of trust extends into his daily life as an interior designer, where he frequently finds himself second-guessing his physical capabilities and reactions. Moreover, John’s sense of identity has been profoundly shaken. The trauma has left him feeling like a different person, unsure of who he is or how to navigate the world post-accident. "I feel like I don’t know myself anymore," he often says with a mix of frustration and sadness. This loss of self has significantly impacted his relationships; he no longer feels confident in his ability to connect with others on the same level as before. The most pervasive negative appraisal John carries is that he has been permanently changed for the worse. "I have permanently changed for the worse," he often tells himself, a belief that has colored his entire outlook on life post-accident. He is convinced that the trauma has left an indelible mark, affecting not just his physical well-being but also his emotional and psychological state. John’s triggers continue to be a significant part of his daily experience. In his work as an interior designer, he often encounters clients who discuss their own experiences with car accidents or describe scenes involving vehicles. These conversations are particularly distressing for John, as they bring back the traumatic memories in full force, leaving him feeling helpless and overwhelmed. Despite these challenges, it is only recently that John has begun to seek help. The cumulative effect of his symptoms has taken a toll on both his personal life and professional work. He found himself increasingly isolated, avoiding social gatherings and professional events where conversations about accidents might arise. What finally brought him to therapy was the realization that he could no longer ignore the profound impact these experiences were having on his life. John is most afraid of being trapped in a cycle of fear and uncertainty forever, unable to reclaim the sense of self he once had. Yet, he also harbors hope that with the right support, he can begin to rebuild his trust in himself and regain some semblance of normalcy in his daily life.
